target.title: Silent Speech Sentence Recognition with Six-Axis Accelerometers using Conformer and CTC Algorithm

read.pdf: Fig. 1–4 captions/axes and Table 1; Fig. 3 plots visually inspected

entries.text: The proposed approach combines six-axis facial-motion sensing with Conformer and CTC for dynamic sentence segmentation and recognition.
entries.condition: Method contribution as described in the introduction; no external code is linked in the paper.
entries.quote:
A Conformer-based neural network with the
Connectionist-Temporal-Classification algorithm gains con-
textual understanding and translates the non-acoustic signals into words sequences.

entries.text: The authors claim theirs is the first SSI method to dynamically segment and recognize sentences.
entries.condition: Novelty claim is qualified as the authors' knowledge; no systematic search protocol is reported.
entries.quote: To the best of our knowledge, no prior study has reported the SSI method to segment and recognize sentences dynamically.

entries.text: The method is presented as dynamic contextual segmentation and recognition rather than static whole-sentence classification.
entries.condition: The paper evaluates on a restricted recorded vocabulary; see dataset entries.

entries.text: The discussion characterizes the system as dynamically recognizing arbitrary silent sentences through autonomous segmentation and identification.
entries.condition: The recorded evaluation vocabulary consists of 16 English words, two English sentences, and eight Chinese phrases; the paper does not test unrestricted arbitrary sentences.
entries.quote:
The strength of the proposed method lies in its ability to dy-
namically recognize arbitrary silent sentences by autonomous segmentation and identification.

entries.text: The conclusion reports average accuracy of 97.17% at both word and sentence levels.
entries.condition: The abstract calls this a test result; the paper does not explicitly bind it to the named 70:15:15 test split or state test-subset composition, evaluation sample unit, session split, seed/repeated-run count, CTC search method, or LM use. Cohort/tasks/sensor/repetitions and training are in t20–t31; omissions in t42–t51.
entries.quote: The model achieves an average accuracy of 97.17% at both word and sentence levels, demonstrating strong performance on classification and generalization.

entries.text: Results report average classification accuracy of 97.24% on words.
entries.condition: Sec. 3.1 reports this average and the abstract calls the 97.17% headline a test result, but the paper does not explicitly map this value to the named 70:15:15 test split; cohort/tasks/sensor/repetitions and training are in t20–t31, while session split, seed/repeated-run count, aggregation, CTC search method, and LM use are not stated (t42–t51).
entries.quote: It attains an average classification accuracy of 97.24% on words and 97.16% on sentences.

entries.text: Results report average classification accuracy of 97.16% on sentences.
entries.condition: Sec. 3.1 reports this average and the abstract calls the 97.17% headline a test result, but the paper does not explicitly map this value to the named 70:15:15 test split; cohort/tasks/sensor/repetitions and training are in t20–t31, while session split, seed/repeated-run count, aggregation, CTC search method, and LM use are not stated (t42–t51).
entries.quote: It attains an average classification accuracy of 97.24% on words and 97.16% on sentences.

entries.text: The conclusion's wording assigns the same 97.17% average to both word and sentence levels, unlike the separate 97.24% and 97.16% results in Sec. 3.1.
entries.condition: Internal numerical inconsistency; the conclusion gives no separate level-specific values.
entries.quote: The model achieves an average accuracy of 97.17% at both word and sentence levels, demonstrating strong performance on classification and generalization.

entries.text: The paper cites 94.65 ± 2.54% as a previous-study result, citing reference [9].
entries.unit: % accuracy (the meaning of ± is not specified here)
entries.condition: Prior result attributed to [9], a three-axis accelerometer SSI using a deep neural network; this paper gives no matched dataset, split, participants, metric protocol, or head-to-head comparison conditions.

entries.text: The abstract characterizes existing silent-speech recognition methods as typically achieving 85%–95% accuracy.
entries.condition: Broad author-stated range for existing methods; no methods, datasets, or evaluation conditions are enumerated alongside this range.

entries.text: Accuracy is defined as correctly recognized words divided by total words in a sentence or dataset, not as an explicitly defined exact-sentence-match rate.
entries.condition: This definition is used in a paper reporting both word and sentence accuracy; the sentence-level aggregation protocol is not further defined.
entries.quote: Accuracy is calculated as the ratio of correctly recognized words to the total words in a sentence or dataset.

entries.text: Figure 3(a) plots sentence lengths 1–19; the caption says accuracy remains above 90% as length increases.
entries.unit: % accuracy; sentence-length values on the x-axis (unit not separately labeled)
entries.condition: Fig. 3(a) bars/error bars; individual plotted values are not printed numerically, and the paper does not explain how the 19 lengths relate to the two English sentences and eight Chinese phrases in the dataset description.
entries.quote: The accuracy remains above 90% even when the length increases.

entries.text: Average accuracy under the paper's standard condition is reported as over 95%.
entries.condition: Standard condition across participants; the paper does not define the split or speaker-overlap protocol for this condition, and exact per-participant values are not printed in the text.

entries.text: The blind cross-participant accuracy is said to vary among individuals; the paper does not print exact blind scores in the prose.
entries.condition: Blind scenario is described as training across different participants for evaluation on unseen subjects; exact held-out-subject protocol and exact scores are not reported in text.

entries.text: Few-shot personalization is reported to raise accuracy to over 90%.
entries.condition: Participant-specific samples are added in the few-shot scenario; number of samples per participant, selection protocol, split, and exact scores are not specified.

entries.text: Mean accuracy across single-channel configurations ranges from 90.22% to 93.19%.
entries.condition: Single channel, Fig. 4(a); evaluation dataset, split, subject aggregation, and repetitions are not separately specified for this ablation.

entries.text: Two or three channels are reported above 95%, with a 1.5 percentage-point reduction compared with six channels.
entries.unit: % accuracy; the 1.5% reduction's relative-versus-percentage-point basis is unspecified
entries.condition: Channel-count ablation in Fig. 4(b); exact value by channel count, test partition, and aggregation are not stated in the text.

entries.text: Single-gyroscope-axis accuracy is 92.39%–93.39%, while single-accelerometer-axis accuracy is 87.62%–92.42%; authors attribute the difference as likely due to rotational articulation.
entries.condition: Single-axis evaluation in Fig. 4(c); axes 1–3 are accelerometer and axes 4–6 gyroscope; partition and aggregation details are not stated.
entries.quote: gyroscope data (92.39–93.39%) consistently outperformed accelerometer data (87.62–92.42%)

entries.text: Two axes achieve 95.37% accuracy versus 95.57% with all six axes.
entries.condition: Axis-count ablation in Fig. 4(d); axes chosen for the two-axis result and evaluation split are not identified in the text.

entries.text: Sensing uses six accelerometer channels, each recording three-axis acceleration and three-axis gyroscope data, at 50 Hz from facial placements.
entries.condition: Wearable facial-motion sensor system shown in Fig. 1.
entries.quote: The test was conducted using six accelerometers (channels).

entries.text: The experiment includes one laryngect participant and three undergraduates, four participants in total.
entries.condition: Single described test cohort; no detailed demographics or participant-wise task allocation is provided.
entries.quote: One laryngect and three undergraduates participated in the test to evaluate the performance of the proposed method.

entries.text: The recorded label set is 16 English words (Afternoon, Thanks, Beautiful, Wait, Breakfast, Want, Drink, Water, Hello, Welcome, Please, What, Sorry, Wonder, Test, Wonderful), two English sentences (“Drink water.” and “Hello, please wait.”), and eight Chinese phrases: Tengtong (Hurt), Fanshen (Turn over), Xiachuang (Getting out of bed), Henkaixin (Very happy), Xiexieni (Thank you), Woyaoheshui (I want to drink water), Woxiangchifan (I want to have a meal), Tianqizhenhao (What nice weather).
entries.condition: Fixed, small recorded task vocabulary rather than open vocabulary; phrase/sentence tokenization and the precise CTC target vocabulary are not fully specified.

entries.text: Words are repeated 100 times with 80-point windows; sentences/phrases use 180-point windows and 30 repetitions; the word sample is 80 × 6 × 6.
entries.value: 100 repetitions/word; 80 points/word; 30 repetitions/sentence or phrase; 180 points; 80×6×6 sample
entries.unit: repetitions; sampling points; window × channels × axes

entries.condition: The paper does not state whether the split is by sample, utterance, session, or participant, nor whether it is randomized or stratified.
entries.quote: The dataset is split 70:15:15 into training, validation, and test sets.

entries.value: 10-fold; noise standard deviation 1/3 of original values

entries.text: Preprocessing uses a three-point moving average, fourth-order Butterworth high-pass filter with 2 Hz cutoff, z-score normalization, and flattening to 36 × window size (80 for words, 180 for sentences).
entries.unit: smoothing points; filter order; Hz; flattened dimensions
entries.condition: Preprocessing specified in Sec. 2.2; scope and fitting data for z-score statistics are not specified separately (see t39).
entries.quote: The data were preprocessed using moving average (3-point smoothing), a 4th-order Butterworth high-pass filter at the 2Hz cutoff frequency to remove motion artifacts, and z-score normalization.

entries.text: The network uses three convolutional blocks and maps 30 input channels to 128 hidden dimensions in the first block; the third block downsamples.
entries.condition: Paper separately says preprocessing flattens to 36 × window size; relationship between that 36-feature input and the stated 30 input channels is not explained.

entries.text: CTC is used to ignore irrelevant input frames and map multiple frames to output sequences.

entries.quote: The model was trained to minimize the sum of CTC loss and Cross-Entropy loss, using the Adams optimizer.

questions.q: Which accuracy should the review report for word and sentence performance?
questions.answer: Sec. 3.1 reports 97.24% for words and 97.16% for sentences, while the conclusion says 97.17% at both levels. Report the section-specific values and flag the conclusion inconsistency; the exact test split for these scores is not stated.

questions.q: Are the 97.17% result and the cited prior results a controlled, comparable test?
questions.answer: No matched comparison protocol is reported. The 94.65 ± 2.54% figure is attributed to reference [9], and the 85%–95% range is broad; datasets, splits, participants, and metric conditions are not aligned in this paper.

questions.q: What does the paper establish about generalization to unseen users and few-shot adaptation?
questions.answer: It describes an unseen-subject blind scenario with accuracy varying across individuals, reports over 90% after adding participant-specific data, and states over 95% in the standard condition. Exact blind scores, few-shot sample counts, and full split details are absent.

questions.q: Is sentence accuracy an exact-sentence-match metric, and what are the test conditions?
questions.answer: The stated formula counts correctly recognized words divided by total words; an exact-sentence-match definition is not given. The paper states a 70:15:15 split but does not map headline results to the test partition or explain speaker overlap in the standard split.

questions.q: What implementation and evaluation details remain unavailable from the paper?
questions.answer: No code link is supplied. Missing items include random seeds/repeated runs, validation-set selection use, z-score statistic scope, exact few-shot sample count, CTC search method, external LM status, and chance baseline.

questions.q: Does the described preprocessing dimension agree with the network input dimension?
questions.answer: The paper says samples are flattened to 36 × window size, while the first convolutional block maps 30 input channels to 128 hidden dimensions; it does not explain this difference.

questions.q: Which earlier works decode silent sentences with CTC or build sentence training data from concatenated words, and how do they test (comparators for M03, M05, M06)?
questions.answer: Free-model reader returned a server error; passages located by targeted search in the source texts of the five comparators (entries c1-c17).

questions.q: Triage: are open-vocabulary or continuous silent-sentence recognizers (Gaddy & Klein, Meltzner 2018, Benster 2024) in the wiki, and do they decide the M06 novelty and state of the art?
questions.answer: Meltzner 2018 (doi-10.1088-1741-2552-aac965) and Benster 2024 (arxiv-2403.05583) are in the wiki; passages read (c30-c32). Gaddy & Klein 2020/2021 are in the wiki but are voicing (synthesis) papers whose benchmark is covered through Benster; not cited.
